synopsis: BLUF puts the conclusion and requested decision first; the booklet recommends a one-to-two-page executive brief so leaders can grasp the decision, confidence and risks quickly [f16444, f10152, f9995]. For this validation plan, the brief should specify what will and will not exist by August or September 2027, P50 and P80 dates, deadline probability, top risks, stop conditions, fallback and required executive actions; the glossary additionally asks for separate preparation and delivery dates and descoping to keep P80 within the deadline [f10151, f16323]. The first page should expose the hardest uncertainty and fallback rather than lead with promised savings, while all seven skeptical reviewers need a credibility map linking safety claims to evidence, model-validation data, uncertainty and acceptance authority [f16454, f11158, f16451]. Technical readers need the underlying reasoning, assumptions, coverage, acceptance thresholds and disputes, with progressive disclosure supporting either a 12–15-page main body or a two-page brief plus roughly 25–35 core pages [f16448, f9994, f16466]. These formats and lengths remain opinion-based rather than proven routes to programme approval or success, although experiments found numeric ranges preserved trust better than verbal hedges [f9853, f10315, f9474].
